summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles is resolved: the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct. Those articles reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy.

Enforcement against same-sex couples has historically run through public-order offences rather than a sodomy statute. A former law criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme. In 2012 police broke up the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with the support of religious leaders.

Transgender people cannot change their legal gender and name to reflect their gender identity. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility of changing their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was among the 35 and subsequently changed her name. The decree addressed names only, not legal gender recognition.

Family law statutes recognise no legal status between same-sex persons, neither marriage nor marriage-like relationships. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55, under which the State shall promote and protect family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 (Private International Law) could justify recognition of a foreign same-sex marriage, since marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, national law or domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage; several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it, but no implementing legislation is sourced here.

Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in areas including health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations, so many LGBTQ people feel the need to remain in the closet. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Citizens have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programmes for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos.

The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations hold significant sway in both public policy and prevailing attitudes surrounding LGBTQ rights. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, and only a plurality of 5% believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

Organised opposition is visible and directed at visible LGBTQ figures. Former openly gay U.S. Ambassador Wally Brewster (2013-2017) was regularly insulted by religious leaders and some politicians, and evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." The backlash against him after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo included attacks on LGBT Dominicans, showing organised domestic opposition; his departure in 2017 left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence, including speaking at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016, and his tenure exposed a polarised climate.

Advocacy infrastructure exists. COTRAVETD (Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers), co-founded in 2004, is led by executive director Nairovi Castillo, who has given first-hand accounts of trans struggles in the country. In April 2017 more than 300 activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo, where Dominican government officials spoke.

The Dominican Republic has accepted UPR recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the accepted record carries no domestic implementation detail.
tangentialFactors:
The Dominican Republic's position sits within a wider regional pattern in which constitutional courts have reviewed residual sodomy provisions and found them inoperative or discriminatory, but where family-law recognition has not followed. The 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion applies to parties to the American Convention, and Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it; whether the Dominican Republic is a party to that Convention and how the opinion binds it is not resolved in the sources here.

Public-order policing, rather than a sodomy statute, has been the operative mechanism against visible same-sex couples, which means the practical risk to a visitor attaches to public displays of affection and to participation in Pride events rather than to private conduct. The 2012 arrest of Pride marchers on a national-flag charge illustrates how incidental offences can be used against LGBTQ assembly.

Religious institutions function as an organised political force rather than a background cultural factor: evangelical groups mounted a petition to expel a foreign ambassador, and religious leaders have supported crackdowns on visible LGBTQ signs. A visitor should expect official hostility to be voiced openly by clerics and some politicians, not confined to private opinion.

Public opinion polling from 2017 indicates a majority supporting criminalisation of same-sex relationships and near-unanimous opposition to legal gender change, which bears on how police and officials are likely to exercise discretion in any encounter.

Transgender Dominicans cannot obtain legal gender recognition; the June 2018 executive decree of President Danilo Medina opened a name-change route for 35 individuals, including television journalist Mía Cepeda, but did not alter the legal gender marker. No general legal gender recognition procedure is sourced.

Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, but this protection is confined to the HIV/AIDS context. Outside it, discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity remains lawful in health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations.

Same-sex couples hold no recognised legal status. The 2010 constitutional amendment's Article 55 commits the State to promote and protect family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman, and same-sex households receive none of the rights attached to opposite-sex marriage. Article 41 of Law 544-14 (Private International Law) may permit recognition of a marriage validly celebrated abroad, but no sourced case law or implementing practice confirms that this has been applied to same-sex couples.

Community organisations include COTRAVETD, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, co-founded in 2004 and directed by Nairovi Castillo, and Amigos Siempre Amigos, which runs HIV/AIDS-focused programming. Health care for LGBTQ Dominicans has generally concentrated on HIV/AIDS education delivered through such non-governmental organisations rather than through state services.

The Dominican Republic has accepted UPR recommendations concerning intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The accepted record shows no domestic implementation detail, so the practical status of these commitments is unresolved.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Dominican Republic is a party to the American Convention on Human Rights and whether the Inter-American Court's 9 January 2018 advisory opinion is binding or persuasive there; the sources assert only that several Dominican legal experts say it must be implemented.

Unresolved: whether Article 41 of Law 544-14 has ever been applied to recognise a same-sex foreign marriage. The provision's text is sourced; no decision or registry practice is.

Unresolved: the scope of the June 2018 executive decree beyond the 35 named individuals, and whether any subsequent procedure for legal gender change has opened. The inventory records only the single decree.

Not sourced: any hate-crime statute covering offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity, and any independent complaint or oversight mechanism for police conduct against LGBTQ people. The 1997 repeal of the "decorum and good behaviour" offence and the 2011 anti-discrimination provision in the HIV/AIDS law are documented; a general hate-crime framework is not.
